title: Me and You
description: Say who you are and where you are from, ask someone's name, and point at yourself, the listener and a third person with the right pronoun — all without a verb 'to be', because Sanaa Arabic does not use one.
approach: GPA Phase 1 → 2. First productive lesson: the learner builds two-word sentences (أنا طالب، هو من عدن) from pronoun cards and noun cards, hearing each before saying it.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 on the listen-and-tap quiz and one recorded self-introduction (name + origin)
can_do: Say who you are and where you are from
Point at yourself, the listener and a third person with the right pronoun

grammar.title: Five people: أنا، أنت، أنتي، هو، هي
grammar.explanation: Sanaa has a separate 'you' for a man (أنت, said ant with no vowel on the end) and for a woman (أنتي anti). He is هو and she is هي. Aden splits 'I' into أنا for a man and أني for a woman, but Sanaa uses أنا for everyone. For a group you will hear إحنا 'we', أنتو 'you all' and هم 'they' — recognise them now, use them later.

examples.english: Are you from Aden? (to a man)
Are you a student? (to a woman)
He is my friend and she is his sister

grammar.title: No 'is': pronoun + word makes a sentence
grammar.explanation: In the present there is no word for 'am', 'is' or 'are'. Put a person next to a name, a place or a describing word and the sentence is finished: أنا طالب 'I am a student', هي من تعز 'she is from Taʿizz', الشاهي حار 'the tea is hot'. To ask a question you simply raise your voice at the end — no extra word is needed. The question word can sit at the end, Sanaa style: أنت من وين؟

culture.title: Names, fathers and titles
culture.note: A Yemeni introduces himself with his first name, and often his father's and grandfather's after it — محمد علي سالم. Friends call each other by first name; a man with a son is respectfully أبو + the son's name (أبو أحمد), and you may hear people ask for him that way. You will be called by titles before anyone knows your name: يا حاج to an older man, يا شيخ half-jokingly to any man, يا عم or يا خال 'uncle' to someone older, يا أستاذ to anyone educated-looking. Answer to all of them; none is a mistake.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Same word for a man or a woman in Sanaa. Aden women say أني — recognise it, do not copy it. Short a at the end, not the long aa of MSA reading.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pointing at his own chest with his thumb, plain background.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa says ant with no vowel on the end — the ta closes the word. Used to one man; to a group or respectfully to an elder it becomes أنتو.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pointing forward at a second man, who points back at himself.
vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviews: the interviewer addressing a man.

vocabulary.teaching_note: To one woman. The -i on the end is the same feminine -i the learner heard in لو سمحتي. Its suffix cousin in Sanaa is -ish (اسمش, حالش).
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman in a colourful Sanaa shawl being addressed by another woman, who points toward her.

example.english: Where are you from? (to a woman)

vocabulary.video_hint: A woman being addressed directly; family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Also 'it' for any masculine thing: الخبز — هو حار. Pronounced huu or huw; some Sanaa speakers say hu with a short vowel.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two people looking toward a third man standing a little apart, one pointing at him.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone talking about a third person visible on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Also 'it' for any feminine thing — every word ending in ة: السيارة — هي جديدة. Pronounced hii or hiy.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two people looking toward a woman standing a little apart, one gesturing toward her.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone talking about a woman visible on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two syllables in Sanaa: i-sim. With endings it shrinks: اسمي ismi, اسمك ismak, اسمش ismish (to a woman), اسمه isma.
vocabulary.image_scene: A name badge on a shirt pocket, blank except for a line.
vocabulary.video_hint: Introductions: اسمي / اسمه said with a person in frame.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The whole sentence is just اسمي + your name — no 'is'. This is the first thing a learner produces in front of a native, so it is drilled until automatic.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with a hand on his chest, mouth open mid-word, a speech bubble with a blank line.

example.english: My name is Salem, and you?

vocabulary.video_hint: The opening of any vlog or interview: اسمي + name.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ايش is the Yemeni 'what'. To a woman in Sanaa: ايش اسمش. Older Sanaa speakers keep the classical ما اسمك؟ — recognise it if you hear it. Word order is loose: اسمك ايش؟ is equally natural.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with a questioning expression pointing at the person opposite him.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'From' a place: من صنعاء، من تعز، من بريطانيا. Watch the spelling trap: the same letters read man mean 'who?' in Sanaa — context and vowel keep them apart.
vocabulary.image_scene: An arrow leaving a small map pin and pointing toward a figure, the pin labelled with a city skyline.
vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone saying where they or a thing is from.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Add your city or country and you have introduced yourself. Yemenis will ask this within a minute of meeting you and will want the city, not just the country.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young woman pointing to herself and then to a country outline on a small map.

example.english: I am from London, and you?

vocabulary.video_hint: Self-introductions naming a hometown; travel vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'We are honoured.' Said after the names are exchanged, with a handshake. فرصة سعيدة also works; the reply to either is الشرف لي 'the honour is mine' or simply the same phrase back.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men shaking hands with their left hands on their chests, both smiling.
vocabulary.video_hint: The moment after names are exchanged in an introduction.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A man is طالب, a woman طالبة — the first noun the learner sees take the feminine ة. The ط is voiced in Sanaa, so it sounds close to d. Also the word to use for yourself: أنا طالب عربي 'I am a student of Arabic'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with a backpack and a book outside a university gate.

example.english: I am a student in Sanaa

vocabulary.video_hint: University or school vlogs; someone saying أنا طالب.

sound_spotlight.explanation: An s made with the tongue pulled back and the mouth hollow — it darkens the vowel after it. The city's own name is the anchor: ṣan-, not san-.
Between vowels ع is a squeeze in the throat that the vowels flow through. Both Yemeni cities carry it; say them slowly and feel the throat close.
Sanaa keeps vowel length strictly: أنا has two short a's, باب one long aa held twice as long. Hearing them side by side makes the length audible before it is ever explained.

lesson_sequence.detail: A café table in Sanaa: two strangers about to meet. One line of English: by the end you will introduce yourself.
The five pronouns as tapping targets on one illustration — tap the speaker, the listener, the man, the woman; audio plays each time.
The remaining seven cards with illustration and audio; second pass with English.
Drag a pronoun card next to a noun or place card (أنا + طالب, هي + من تعز) and hear the sentence spoken. No 'is' to add — the app points this out once.
All twelve, audio only, four-image grid.
Record اسمي … أنا من … and hear it next to the model. Feedback on ص and ع only.
Counter rolls up. Nudge: introduce yourself in Arabic to the next Arabic speaker you meet.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say your own introduction out loud once now: اسمي … أنا من … . That is a complete Sanaa conversation opener.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. First full production.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask someone ايش اسمك؟ today — a tutor, a shopkeeper, a language partner — and answer their question back with تشرفنا.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Uses the question and the reply in one real exchange.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor which city they are from and whether they say ant or anta, ana or ani — and where each is heard.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Makes the Sanaa/Aden pronoun difference concrete.

video_needs.scene: A self-introduction: vloggers opening with اسمي and their city, street interviews asking name and origin.
